raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular myocardial deposition of misfolded protein fibrils. Clinically important forms are immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL), a plasma-cell dyscrasia with rapid cardiac toxicity, and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), caused either by pathogenic TTR variants (ATTRv) or age-related wild-type transthyretin deposition (ATTRwt) [1–3]. Autopsy and clinical series show that ATTRwt is common in very old adults and increasingly recognized among patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, severe aortic stenosis, carpal tunnel syndrome, and unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy [4–8]. ATTRv prevalence varies by ancestry and mutation; the Val122Ile variant is particularly relevant in people of West African ancestry and is associated with adverse outcomes [9].

Pathobiology differs by subtype. In AL, circulating amyloidogenic light chains appear directly cardiotoxic in addition to forming fibrils, explaining the often abrupt heart failure trajectory. In ATTR, tetramer dissociation, monomer misfolding, and fibril deposition lead to progressive ventricular stiffening, atrial myopathy, conduction disease, and sometimes low-flow aortic stenosis. The clinical phenotype is often discordant with standard heart failure markers: patients may have increased wall thickness, small ventricular cavities, low stroke volume, preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, restrictive filling, right-sided congestion, autonomic dysfunction, and disproportionate elevations of natriuretic peptides or troponins [3,10].

Diagnosis requires both recognition and amyloid typing. Red flags include unexplained ventricular wall thickening, low QRS voltage relative to wall thickness, pseudoinfarct ECG pattern, atrial arrhythmias, conduction block, biceps tendon rupture, lumbar spinal stenosis, nephrotic-range proteinuria, neuropathy, macroglossia, and prior bilateral carpal tunnel release. Serum free light chains with serum and urine immunofixation are essential first-line tests, because missing AL amyloidosis can be fatal. In patients without monoclonal protein, grade 2–3 cardiac uptake on technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy can establish ATTR cardiomyopathy noninvasively [11]. This approach was built on observations that DPD and pyrophosphate scintigraphy strongly differentiate ATTR from AL when interpreted with monoclonal-protein testing [12,13].

Echocardiography typically shows concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, valve thickening, pericardial effusion, restrictive diastolic filling, and reduced tissue Doppler velocities. Longitudinal strain often shows relative apical sparing, a useful but not definitive pattern [17]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization: diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal gadolinium kinetics, elevated native T1, and extracellular volume expansion support diagnosis and provide prognostic information [14–16]. Endomyocardial or extracardiac biopsy remains necessary when AL is suspected, scintigraphy is equivocal, monoclonal gammopathy coexists, or rare amyloid types are possible; typing should ideally use mass spectrometry or validated immunohistochemistry.

Prognosis is driven mainly by cardiac involvement. In AL, troponin, NT-proBNP, and the involved–uninvolved free light-chain difference define widely used staging systems [18,19]. In ATTRwt and ATTRv, natriuretic peptide, troponin, renal function, and functional capacity stratify risk, but disease course is generally slower than cardiac AL [20,21]. Accurate staging informs urgency: AL cardiac amyloidosis is a hematologic emergency, whereas ATTR care emphasizes early disease-modifying therapy before advanced low-output heart failure.

Treatment has changed substantially. AL therapy targets the plasma-cell clone, with rapid suppression of light-chain production as the central goal. Daratumumab added to cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone improves hematologic and organ responses and has become a key first-line regimen for many patients [22]. Supportive cardiac care is equally important but challenging: loop diuretics and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are mainstays, while beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors are often poorly tolerated because of fixed stroke volume, hypotension, and autonomic dysfunction. Digoxin and nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers require caution.

For ATTR cardiomyopathy, tafamidis stabilizes transthyretin and reduces mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations, establishing disease modification as standard for eligible symptomatic patients [23]. Gene-silencing therapies such as patisiran and inotersen reduce hepatic transthyretin production and were first proven in ATTR polyneuropathy, with cardiac signals supporting broader investigation [24,25]. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing and next-generation stabilizers such as acoramidis/AG10 illustrate an expanding therapeutic landscape [26,27]. Management also includes anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, a low threshold for evaluating atrial mechanical dysfunction, pacemakers for clinically significant conduction disease, and selective defibrillator use because sudden death often reflects electromechanical dissociation rather than ventricular tachyarrhythmia.

Earlier recognition is now the major challenge. Screening selected populations—older patients with HFpEF, low-flow aortic stenosis, unexplained hypertrophy, neuropathy, or carpal tunnel syndrome—can uncover treatable disease [28,29]. Multidisciplinary pathways linking cardiology, hematology, neurology, nephrology, imaging, and genetics are recommended to accelerate typing, initiate therapy, counsel families with ATTRv, and monitor response [30].
